steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on MultiMon, a system that uses language models to automatically find failures of text-to-image and other text-based multimodal systems. Motivate the problem, explain how the system works, and summarize the main results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Problem: multimodal systems fail at deployment despite testing
2. Goals: systematic and human-compatible evaluation
3. MultiMon overview
4. Scraping individual failures via erroneous agreement
5. Language models for systematic failures + steering
6. Evaluation setup and CLIP results
7. Transfer to downstream systems, safety filters, outlook

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Problem
- text-based multimodal systems: produce images, 3d scenes, videos from text
- tested extensively in development, still routinely fail at deployment
- part of the reason: evaluators can't anticipate/test all failures beforehand

2. Goals
- want evaluation that is systematic + human-compatible
- systematic: look into long tail of behaviors; no a priori assumptions about what to look for; not bottlenecked by human labor
- human-compatible: useful to designer; describe patterns, not just examples; steerable to designer's goals

3. MultiMon (Section 3)
- uses LLMs to identify failures of multimodal systems
- scrape individual failures from corpus -> categorize into systematic failures (natural language) -> generate novel instances
- autonomous, improves as LMs scale, failures transfer across multimodal systems

4. Erroneous agreement
- two inputs, same output, different semantics -> at least one wrong
- same output test: compare CLIP embeddings (many multimodal models encode inputs with CLIP before generating)
- skips expensive decoding step -> can scrape large corpora tractably

5. Systematic failures
- GPT-4 turns scraped failures into systematic failures = generalizable natural-language descriptions of failure patterns
- uses: understand behavior qualitatively; generate new instances
- steering towards attributes missing from corpus but important downstream, e.g. "salient to self-driving"

6. Evaluation (Section 4)
- quantity: count of systematic failures; quality: fraction of new instances with high CLIP similarity
- 14 systematic failures of CLIP text-encoder, over one thousand new individual failures
- examples: negation, spatial differences, numerical differences, role ambiguity, quantifiers, more
- 12 of 14 give high-similarity pairs at least half the time; 7 at least 75% of the time

7. Transfer (Figure 1, Section 5)
- transfer to text-to-image, text-to-video, text-to-3d
- five text-to-image systems: Stable Diffusion 1.5, 2.1, XL, DALL-E, Midjourney 5.1; three released within a month of writing
- manual evaluation: 80.0% of MultiMon pairs vs 20.5% for baseline
- evading commercial safety filters (Section 7)
- pipeline simple and general, possible foundation for broader automatic evaluation

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Text-based multimodal systems that produce images, 3d scenes, and videos from text get tested a lot for failures while they are being developed, but they still routinely fail when they are deployed. Part of the reason for this gap is that evaluators have a hard time anticipating and testing for all of the possible failures ahead of time.

To close this gap, we want evaluation systems for multimodal models that are systematic and also human-compatible. A systematic evaluation has to look into the long tail of possible model behaviors, so the system can't assume beforehand what behaviors it should look for, and it can't be bottlenecked by human labor. A human-compatible evaluation has to be useful to the system designer, so it should describe patterns of behavior and not just give examples, and it should be steerable towards what the designer wants.

We build a system called MultiMon that tries to meet these goals by using large language models to find failures of multimodal systems (Section 3). MultiMon scrapes individual failures from a corpus, then it categorizes them into systematic failures which are written in natural language, and then it generates new instances in a flexible way. MultiMon works on its own without humans, it gets better as language models scale, and the failures it finds transfer across a range of multimodal systems.

For scraping individual failures systematically, MultiMon uses erroneous agreement. The observation is that if two inputs give the same output but have different semantics, then at least one of them has to be wrong. To test if two inputs give the same output we can compare their CLIP embeddings, because many multimodal models encode their inputs with CLIP before they generate outputs. Using CLIP similarity means we skip the expensive decoding step of these models, and this is what lets us scrape large corpora for failures in a tractable way.

5. Systematic failures
- GPT-4 turns scraped failures into systematic failures = generalizable natural-language descriptions of failure patterns
- uses: understand behavior qualitatively; generate new instances
- steering towards attributes missing from corpus but important downstream, e.g. "salient to self-driving"

6. Evaluation (Section 4)
- quantity: count of systematic failures; quality: fraction of new instances with high CLIP similarity
- 14 systematic failures of CLIP text-encoder, over one thousand new individual failures
- examples: negation, spatial differences, numerical differences, role ambiguity, quantifiers, more
- 12 of 14 give high-similarity pairs at least half the time; 7 at least 75% of the time

7. Transfer (Figure 1, Section 5)
- transfer to text-to-image, text-to-video, text-to-3d
- five text-to-image systems: Stable Diffusion 1.5, 2.1, XL, DALL-E, Midjourney 5.1; three released within a month of writing
- manual evaluation: 80.0% of MultiMon pairs vs 20.5% for baseline

- pipeline simple and general, possible foundation for broader automatic evaluation

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Text-based multimodal systems that produce images, 3d scenes, and videos from text get tested a lot for failures while they are being developed, but they still routinely fail when they are deployed. Part of the reason for this gap is that evaluators have a hard time anticipating and testing for all of the possible failures ahead of time.

To close this gap, we want evaluation systems for multimodal models that are systematic and also human-compatible. A systematic evaluation has to look into the long tail of possible model behaviors, so the system can't assume beforehand what behaviors it should look for, and it can't be bottlenecked by human labor. A human-compatible evaluation has to be useful to the system designer, so it should describe patterns of behavior and not just give examples, and it should be steerable towards what the designer wants.

We build a system called MultiMon that tries to meet these goals by using large language models to find failures of multimodal systems (Section 3). MultiMon scrapes individual failures from a corpus, then it categorizes them into systematic failures which are written in natural language, and then it generates new instances in a flexible way. MultiMon works on its own without humans, it gets better as language models scale, and the failures it finds transfer across a range of multimodal systems.

For scraping individual failures systematically, MultiMon uses erroneous agreement. The observation is that if two inputs give the same output but have different semantics, then at least one of them has to be wrong. To test if two inputs give the same output we can compare their CLIP embeddings, because many multimodal models encode their inputs with CLIP before they generate outputs. Using CLIP similarity means we skip the expensive decoding step of these models, and this is what lets us scrape large corpora for failures in a tractable way.

After that, MultiMon uses language models on top of these scraped failures to produce explanations that are human-compatible. We use GPT-4 to find systematic failures, which are generalizable natural-language descriptions of patterns of failures, starting from the individual failures we scraped. The systematic failures are useful for understanding the behavior of the system qualitatively and also for generating new instances. We can also steer the generation towards specific attributes that are missing from the original corpus but that matter for downstream applications, for example “salient to self-driving”.

We evaluate MultiMon by measuring the quantity and the quality of the systematic failures. For quantity we count how many systematic failures are generated, and for quality we measure what fraction of the new generated instances have high CLIP similarity.

MultiMon finds 14 systematic failures of the CLIP text-encoder, and from these it finds over one thousand new individual failures (Section 4). The systematic failures include failing to encode negation, spatial differences, numerical differences, role ambiguity, quantifiers, and more. They are also high quality: 12 of the 14 systematic failures give pairs with high CLIP similarity at least half the time, and 7 of them give such pairs at least 75% of the time.

The failures of the CLIP text-encoder also transfer to downstream text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3d systems (Figure 1, Section 5). We test the new individual failures from MultiMon on five widely-used text-to-image systems, which are Stable Diffusion 1.5, Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, DALL-E, and Midjourney 5.1, and three of them were released within a month of the writing of this paper. In a manual evaluation, the systems err on 80.0% of the pairs that MultiMon generates, while for a baseline system it is only 20.5%. We also show that MultiMon can help evaluators find inputs that evade commercial safety filters (Section 7). Overall the MultiMon pipeline, which exploits erroneous agreement to scrape individual failures and finds patterns with language models, is simple and general, and it could be a foundation for broader automatic evaluation.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Text-based multimodal systems, which produce images [1], 3d scenes [2], and videos [3] from text, are extensively tested for failures during development, yet still routinely fail at deployment [4]. This gap exists partly because evaluators struggle to anticipate and test for every possible failure beforehand.

To close this gap, we seek evaluation systems for multimodal models that are both systematic and human-compatible. Systematic evaluations must look into the long tail of possible model behaviors; this means the system cannot assume a priori which behaviors to look for, and cannot be bottlenecked by human labor. Human-compatible evaluations must be useful to the system designer; this means they should describe patterns of behavior rather than only giving examples, and they should be steerable towards the designer’s goals.

Towards these desiderata, we construct a system, MultiMon, that uses large language models to identify failures of multimodal systems (Section 3). MultiMon scrapes individual failures from a corpus, categorizes them into systematic failures (expressed in natural language), and then flexibly generates novel instances. MultiMon works autonomously, improves as language models scale, and produces failures that transfer across a range of multimodal systems.

To scrape individual failures systematically, MultiMon exploits erroneous agreement. Specifically, we observe that if two inputs produce the same output but have different semantics, at least one of them must be wrong. We can test whether two inputs produce the same output by comparing their CLIP embeddings, since many multimodal models encode inputs with CLIP before generating outputs. Using CLIP similarity avoids the expensive decoding step of these models, which lets us tractably scrape large corpora for failures.

Building on these scraped individual failures, MultiMon then uses language models to produce human-compatible explanations. Specifically, we use GPT-4 to identify systematic failures, i.e. generalizable natural-language descriptions of patterns of failures, from the scraped individual failures. These systematic failures are useful both for qualitatively understanding system behavior and for generating new instances. We can even steer generation towards specific attributes, e.g. “salient to self-driving”, that are missing from the original corpus but matter for downstream applications.

To evaluate MultiMon, we measure the quantity and quality of the systematic failures. Quantity is the number of systematic failures generated, and quality is the fraction of the new generated instances that have high CLIP similarity.

We find that MultiMon uncovers 14 systematic failures of the CLIP text-encoder, and from them over one thousand new individual failures (Section 4). These include failing to encode negation, spatial differences, numerical differences, role ambiguity, quantifiers, and more. The systematic failures are high quality: 12 of the 14 produce pairs with high CLIP similarity at least half the time, and 7 do so at least 75% of the time.

The failures of the CLIP text-encoder transfer to downstream text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3d systems (Figure 1, Section 5). We assess the new individual failures generated by MultiMon on five widely-used text-to-image systems: Stable Diffusion 1.5, Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, DALL-E, and Midjourney 5.1, three of which were released within a month of the writing of this paper. In a manual evaluation, the systems err on 80.0% of the pairs generated by MultiMon, compared to only 20.5% for a baseline system. We also show that MultiMon can help evaluators find inputs that evade commercial safety filters (Section 7). Overall, the MultiMon pipeline—exploiting erroneous agreement to scrape individual failures and using language models to find patterns—is simple and general, and could serve as a foundation for broader automatic evaluation.
